title: The Doctrine of Dvaitadvaita Vedanta
summary: The Doctrine of Dvaitadvaita Vedanta — A source-conscious study of this subject.
body:
The philosophy of Shri Nimbarkacharya is widely known as Dvaitadvaita Vedanta. The name expresses two related affirmations: the individual self and the world are different from Brahman, and they are also non-different from Brahman. Difference and non-difference are not treated as mutually cancelling alternatives, but as two aspects of one real relationship.

## The aspect of difference

The individual self is conscious, while the world is experienced as non-conscious. The self is associated with agency, experience, knowledge, pleasure and pain; the world is characterised by names, forms and change. Their distinct features are part of experience and are not simply dismissed as unreal or groundless in this account.

## The aspect of non-difference

The self and the world depend upon the Supreme Brahman. Their existence, capacity and continuance are not independent of the ultimate cause. Traditional Vedanta commentaries use illustrations such as clay and a pot, gold and an ornament, or the ocean and its waves to explain the relation: an effect is not unrelated to its cause, while its particular form remains recognisable. Such illustrations assist understanding; they do not replace the philosophical argument.

## Scriptural exposition

The supplied research text refers to Brahma Sutra 3.2.20, 'ubhaya-vyapadeshat tv ahikundalavat', in connection with the Nimbarkite explanation of the relation between the universe and Brahman as difference-and-non-difference. It also cites Shri Nimbarkacharya's Vedanta-Parijata-Saurabha and Shri Srinivasa's Vedanta-Kaustubha. The complete wording, edition and page references must be checked against the original works before a critical publication.

## Spiritual significance

The practical purpose of Dvaitadvaita is to help the individual understand its dependent relationship with the Supreme. This understanding supports devotion, surrender and service. The self is neither an independent reality unrelated to Bhagavan nor devoid of its own distinct identity; its highest good is realised in loving relationship with the Supreme.
